correctness.rationale: Positivity makes the reciprocal-response coordinate a global circle diffeomorphism of the stated circumference. The chain rule gives ∂_u log A=A' and hence the claimed constant-Poisson equations. The tangent half-angle transformation gives A=k²/(1−ε cos t); scaling both derivatives gives k²B∇ℋ. The sum of t_i is a Casimir because the column sums of B vanish. On its zero leaf (not the original phase-sum-zero set), equilibrium means the three values of ε sin t/(1−ε cos t) agree. A nonzero value gives at most two phases by a genuine quadratic in tan(t/2), with t=π excluded; the zero value gives just 0 and π. Two phases must coincide, and substituting (w,w,−2w) yields sin w(2 cos w+1)(1+ε−2ε cos w)=0; the final factor is strictly positive. This exhausts the six candidates. The constrained Hessians are definite at the equal-coordinate points, and at each mixed point the determinant is −ε²(1+3ε)/((1−ε)(1+ε)²). The three values are strictly ordered by the positive product differences in the proof. Near the extrema compactness excludes any other local level components. On each closed band of regular values, ∇h/||∇h||² transports levels diffeomorphically, so the counts persist throughout each indicated open energy interval. The Hamiltonian field is nonzero on each compact circle component, making it one periodic orbit.
residual_risks: The census does not describe other Casimir leaves, nonzero natural frequencies, or the individual connections at the saddle level.

evidence: Pikovsky's general phase-volume result contains the model class; its triad example has A=0.5+sin x, other couplings and nonzero frequencies. broader_coverage.reasoning: Volume conservation does not determine the level topology. The limiting Morse pattern motivates a small-ε comparison; it cannot rule out new equilibria or degeneracy across every finite ε in (0,1).

evidence: Pikovsky's Eq. (9) becomes the exact Winfree vector field after setting all natural frequencies to zero and choosing the frozen response and matrix. Burylko et al.'s trigonometric first integral equals lim h_ε/ε after (p,q)=(φ₁,−φ₂). Their match is not an equality at finite ε: at p=π their integral is identically −1 in q, but exp(−h_ε)=(1+ε)(1−ε²cos²q) there.

originality.rationale: The skew Winfree equations are prior, and the constant-Poisson reduction in their positive-response zero-frequency case is a short consequence. Neither inspected model supplies the exact finite-ε census and levels for this product response over the whole stated interval.
